Matt

> I think this is due to a bug in the code for derived.openCR(). See attached pdf where this is explored for Matt's example.
> I have fixed the bug, rebuilt my working version of the next release (1.2.1) and placed the Windows binary here <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/openCR_1.2.1.zip> and the source code here <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/openCR_1.2.1.tar.gz>.
>
> Jennifer - I'm sorry this took so long; I've not been working on openCR.
>
> Also - Dscale now applies to the session-specific derived D. Other changes noted in News -
> news(package = 'openCR') [after installing package]
>
> Murray
>

> On Wednesday, October 31, 2018 at 2:55:23 AM UTC+13, Matt Rogan wrote:
> > Hi all, I want to follow up on Jennifer's post to see if anyone has new insights. I have been playing around with openCR models and I am trying to make sense of the outputs and derived parameters. I've fit various versions of the model, with different movementmodels, spatial vs. non-spatial, single session vs multi-session capthist, etc and in all cases the parameter estimates are fairly consistent but I don't quite understand the derived results. I am directly estimating phi and f but am also interested in the derived estimate of lambda:
> >
> > In the following case I have a multi-session capthist object with five sessions and each session consisting of a single occasion. Intervals between sessions are specified as c(0.84, 0.75, 1.32, 1.01). For simplicity's sake, I have not included any covariates for parameters.
> >
> > mod <- openCR.fit(igr.ch <http://igr.ch>, type = "JSSAsecrfCL", mask = igr.mask, detectfn = "HHN", distribution = "poisson",
> >                                movementmodel = "exponential", trace = 25)
> >
> > Below are the derived estimates. As Jennifer found, phi is constant across sessions, but f varies. It seems like both should vary based on the interval between sessions, but the variation in f cannot be explained by differences in the interval. There also is a disconnect between the derived estimates of lambda and D. Between sessions 2 and 3 (for example), lambda is greater than 1 but D decreases, while the esa stays the same. I'm not sure what to make of these results. Any clarification or insights would be greatly appreciated. code and input objects attached.
> >
> >
> > mod.drvd <- derived(mod, Dscale = 1e4)
> >
> > mod.drvd$estimates #rounded to three or four digits
> >

> > > Hello,
> > >
> > > I think I am having an issue with calling derived() from the openCR package.  I had experienced a suite of issues using the function on different models, and after trying a bunch of different things to resolve the problems, and exploring the source codes, I think they all stemmed from an inability to properly call the right derived() function.  This is what happens when I try to specify the package for use of derived() on an openCR model:
> > >

> > >
> > > This is confusing to me, as the output using secr::derived() looks like it is appropriate for an openCR model, but with some bugs, described below.  I have tried several times to uninstall and reinstall openCR and Rcpp (I thought the issue might be with the makegkcpp function), and have explored the source codes, but have been unable to resolve the issue. I was able to replicate results for derived() from the openCR source codes for the JSSAsecrbCL model type, as derived() doesn't work at all for those model types, but the openCR.esa() function did not work properly either, so I got stalled when trying to derive D:

> > > It seems to have less obvious issues with non-spatial models, but upon closer examination of the results, there might be issues there too. I have fit a JSSAf model type using the following parameterization:
> > > p~sex, phi~sex, f~t+sex, N~t
> > >
> > > and also used RMark to fit a similar type of model:
> > > p~sex, phi~sex, f~t+sex, f0~t (RMark RDPdfcClosed, which uses the Pradel formulation instead)
> > >
> > > The outputs from openCR, both real and derived are below, followed by the results from RMark. I understand that both phi and f are scaled for the user-specified time intervals (for these results, 10, 1, and 9 for primary sessions).
> > >
> > > But why is phi the same using the predict() and derived() functions, but f is not? It looks like f is somehow scaled incorrectly, as it is the same in the second primary session, when there is a time interval of 1 afterward, but much smaller for the others.  Could this be affecting N estimates, as the openCR derived estimates are very different from the derived estimates using RMark?
> > >
> > > Note, I have an uneven number of secondary sampling occasions in my second primary session for some of my transects, and did not incorporate this into my RMark analysis, but my capthist traps object does have an appropriate usage matrix. messages.subject: Error in fitting models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Using secr.fit function I found a warning message in some of the models I was trying to fit:

M0C <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~1, sigma~1))
MbC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~b, sigma~1))
MtC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~t, sigma~1))
MbtC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~b+t, sigma~1))
MTC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~T, sigma~1))
MBC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~B, sigma~1))
MbkC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~bk, sigma~1))
MBkC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~Bk, sigma~1))
MKC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~K, sigma~1))
MK_NMC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~K, sigma~1),method="Nelder-Mead")
MkC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~k, sigma~1))
Mh2C <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~h2, sigma~1))
Mh2_NMC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~h2, sigma~1),method="Nelder-Mead")
Mh2_NM_SLC <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~h2, sigma~1),method="Nelder-Mead",start=list(D=0.00012,g0=0.24,sigma=3200))
Mh2_NM_SM0C <-secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask=mask_prox, model = list(D~1, g0~h2, sigma~1),method="Nelder-Mead",start=M0)

Here the warning message delivered:

Warning message:
In secr.fit(roe_capthist, mask = mask_prox, model = list(D ~ 1,  :
  possible maximization error: nlm returned code 3. See ?nlm

This is the information given by R about ?nlm : Non linear minimization warning code 3: Last global step failed to locate a point lower than estimate. Either estimate is an approximate local minimum of the function or steptol is too small

Do someone know the meaning of this warning message and if it really affect the results of the fitted models?

Thank you very much for your attention and help,

Amael

messages.subject: Re: Error in fitting models
messages.body_plain:
It has not been a problem in the cases I've examined: proceed with caution. If some variances are missing a model can be re-fitted with model = 'none' and start=previousmodelfit.

You seem to be trying to fit an exhaustive list of detection models. What about all the combinations involving variation in sigma? Basically, I think this is not good practice.

messages.subject: Re: LYNX DISPERSAL
messages.body_plain:
1. See the literature on dispersal. These may help you find other sources:

Fujiwara, M., Anderson, K. E., Neubert, M. G. and Caswell, H. (2006). On the estimation of dispersal kernels from individual mark--recapture data. Environmental and Ecological Statistics 13, 183-197

Nathan, R., Klein, E., Robledo-Arnuncio, J. J. and Revilla, E. (2012). Dispersal kernels: review. In: J. Clobert et al. (eds) Dispersal Ecology and Evolution. Oxford University Press. Pp. 187-210.
2. Dispersal kernels are almost always fat-tailed; so we expect exponential to be the better 'canned' option. Even that is only borderline fat-tailed.
3. Do not expect too much of the models. I haven't yet seen an application of SECR/SCR where I really trust the results for dispersal.
Murray

P.S. I hope your caps topic doesn't start a trend

messages.subject: Re: OpenCR- varying trends
messages.body_plain:
The discrepancy between results from the custom (openCR.bk) and secr.bk models turns out to be real - the custom bk option is not quite right for anything but a CJSsecr model. Technically - the parameter index array (PIA) was incorrect for naive animals. A canned bk predictor is in openCR 1.3.0 due out soon; 1.3.0 also enables valid custom predictors with learned responses (the naive PIA problem).

On Friday, October 26, 2018 at 4:01:56 PM UTC+13, Murray Efford wrote:
> I can't remember why there is no bk model in openCR. For fun I generated one with the custom design data option (see vignette):
>
> makedf.bk <- function (ch, nmix = 1) {
>     ch <- squeeze(ch)
>     # Construct array of logical values TRUE iff caught at k on or before s
>     detected.at.k <- apply(abs(ch), c(1,3), cumsum) > 0
>     # TRUE only if detected at k before occasion s
>     bk <- apply(detected.at.k, 2:3, function(x) {x[which.max(x)] <- FALSE; x})
>     bk <- aperm(bk, c(2,1,3))
>     n <- nrow(ch)
>     S <- ncol(ch)
>     K <- dim(ch)[3]
>     data.frame(bk = insertdim(bk, 1:3, c(n,S,K,nmix)))
> }
>
> ## test against auto bk in secr.fit
> msk <- make.mask(traps(captdata), buffer = 100, type = 'trapbuffer')
> openCR.bk <- openCR.fit(captdata, type = 'secrCL', detectfn = 'HHN', model = lambda0~bk, mask = msk, dframe = makedf.bk(captdata))
> secr.bk <- secr.fit(captdata, CL = TRUE, detectfn = 'HHN', model = lambda0~bk, mask = msk, trace = FALSE)
>
> coef(openCR.bk)
> # beta    SE.beta       lcl        ucl
> # lambda0        -1.2307701 0.12603152 -1.477787 -0.9837529
> # lambda0.bkTRUE  0.1709865 0.19772481 -0.216547  0.5585200
> # sigma           3.3719294 0.04819498  3.277469  3.4663898
> coef(secr.bk)
> # beta    SE.beta        lcl        ucl
> # lambda0        -1.2331212 0.12628479 -1.4806348 -0.9856075
> # lambda0.bkTRUE  0.1782056 0.19810530 -0.2100737  0.5664848
> # sigma           3.3725295 0.04825689  3.2779477  3.4671113
>
> ## close, but not identical (probably a minor numerical issue)
>
> This effect persists from one primary session to the next. The capthist passed to makedf.bk() must already be 'joined' (cast as a single session)
>
>
> On Tuesday, October 23, 2018 at 9:13:59 AM UTC+13, Clayton Lamb wrote:
> > Thanks for the information Murray, and additions from Michelle and John.
> >
> > Michelle, my top models are the same as yours, lambda-~sex*Trap and sigma~sex, and the sigma~sex*Trap model is running right now. All resulting growth rates are comparable regardless of the model, so long as I don’t include the ~b..
> >
> > Cheers,
> > CL
> >
> > > On Oct 18, 2018, at 1:17 PM, Michelle McLellan <mcl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > I am also interested in this topic.
> > >
> > > I have run similar analyses using long term monitoring data where grizzly hair was collected from baited hair traps and rub trees.  The top models for g0 and sigma were the same for two different populations with different trends for density over time.  In both cases the top model (AIC weight>0.96)  had g0~ sex * traptype and sigma ~ sex. This seemed biologically logical because females and males rub with different probabilities and have different home range sizes. Other candidate models did  include sigma~ sex *trap type and various responses to previous capture (b and bk).
> > >
> > > A reviewer suggested that I remove models using sigma ~ traptype (even though it wasn't the top model ) because they could see no biological hypothesis for this. What do you think about that comment? In my example it ended up moot but I could see how there might be an effect.
> > >
> > > Thanks,
> > >
> > > Michelle
> > >
> > > On Wed, Oct 17, 2018 at 2:03 PM Murray Efford <murray...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > For the record, my original offlist reply was
> > > >
> > > > "Nothing much to say here - you are the one close to the data who can figure this out! It is inherently risky (and in my view illogical) to model lambda0 as a function of trap type while keeping sigma constant. Why if ~bk is a good model do you fit ~b?"
> > > >
> > > > I stand by my statement about lambda0 and sigma, which was not directly about compensation. Detection probability is a function of both parameters (not lambda0 alone). Fixing sigma across types only makes sense if you are sure there no broad-sense behavioural effects. In Clayton's case it is entirely possible that the probability of interacting with a detector, given presence at the point, depends on where the detector is in the home range and differs between the two detector types; that would lead to a difference in sigma between types. Remember I was just throwing out cheap advice. Compensation is another story (both relevant and a perhaps red herring).
> > > >
> > > > I had forgotten that openCR does not offer ~bk, but ~b is not a substitute - they are different models usually leading to quite different estimates (~bk often gives estimated densities close to null-model densities). There are also tricky questions about the duration of a learned response - I would skip it.
> > > >
> > > > We have a lot to learn about the behaviour of open spatial models!
> > > >
> > > > Murray
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Wednesday, October 17, 2018 at 2:35:55 PM UTC+13, Clayton Lamb wrote:
> > > > > Hello
> > > > >
> > > > > Foreword: I am reposting so Murray and I can continue this conversation here where it can be documented/used by others. So far he has suggested that I shouldn’t run a model where Lamba0 varies by trap_type without doing the same for sigma. This confuses me a bit, as I don’t expect the spatial scale of the detections to differ between the traps, I just know that one of the two trap types has ~1/4 the detection probability. Does that make sense or am I missing something? Murray also asked why I am using ~b, when I say ~bk usually fit well in our density models, which I only did because I didn’t see a bk option, only b, based on table 5 from the vignette (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/openCR/vignettes/openCR-vignette.pdf)
> > > > >
> > > > > Two questions/observations as I work with the new openCR package:
> > > > >
> > > > > 1) I fit simple models for detection: ~1, ~b, ~ trap_type, ~trap_type+b. We know that our trap types (bait sites and rub trees) differ largely in their detection probability, and we often see the bk variable come out in density models, so these seemed like good candidate models. I found the results (screenshot attached) a bit confusing, as the trap_type variable drops out, and we know that this has a big effect on detection (Lamb et al. 2016 and work by others). I see that the trap variables add much information over the null, but somehow this b variable alone is better explaining the variation in detection than trap type. This seems odd to me. Do you have any insight?
> > > > >
> > > > > 2) My main goal is to estimate trend, and any variation in the trend through time. Just for illustrative purposes, I ran models that allowed for two values of population growth to be estimated, one in the early portion of the study (2006-2012) and one in the later (2012-2013). I ran these models with the ~ trap_type and ~trap_type+b detection variables . Surprisingly (which I say because I find density results from ‘secr’ to be rather insensitive to different detection covariates in my experience), the trend flips either increasing then decreasing, or decreasing then increasing, depending on the detection covariates used (results in screenshot, I use the derived density just to show the trends). This too seemed odd to me, and I found the sensitivity in the results concerning. Previously, we had shown a decline, using non-spatial open models between 2006-2013, so I am surprised to see a possible increase during this period with the inclusion of the b variable. Again, any thoughts on this?
> > > > >
> > > > > Appreciate it,
> > > > > Clayton

messages.subject: secr 3.1.8 - fixed link
messages.body_plain:
secr 3.1.8 is on CRAN. A summary method is provided for fitted models ('secr' objects). The result (try summary (secrdemo.0)) is a list that looks rather like the printed output. It is handy as a compact output from simulations (e.g., better than the default extractfn argument in secrdesign because it includes a raw data summary).  The summary is not exhaustive (e.g., it omits mark-resight) and more components may be added later.

A significant bug  has been fixed (detector usage was ignored for some models with 'multi' detectors). For other changes see here <https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=secr/NEWS>.

messages.subject: Multi-sesison errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,
Hoping for some guidance on a couple issues. I'm working with some pretty sparse grizzly bear hair snare data and trying to pull what I can out of it. We've done two years of pilot program work (2014 and 2015) followed by a very intensive field program in 2017. Due tot he data scarcity I'm trying to work this into a multi-session dataset. For simplicity at this stage I'm using "secr" and haven't started fitting models with openCR just yet. I'm working with 3 sessions, each with their own trap layout. The first two sessions (2014 and 2015) have 2 sampling occassions, and the last session (2017) has 4.

I'm running into two issues that may or may not be related.

1) Data input in the normal format doesn't work when I include a Usage field ("Error in read.traps (file= ...) 'usage fields suggest varying number of occassions). I have tried inputing the data as .csv, .txt. and even .xlsx and always run into this same error. Is there an error with the way I have the data structured? For a while I thought it might be because some of the Usage fields having a leading zero (e.g. "0011"), so the usage for that field may be interpreted as having only 2 values. But I don't think this is the issue. I've eventually done a work around with the attached code where I build the session-specific trap objects separately an import their Usage and covariate fields, and then call a list of those trap objects in the make.capthist function

2) Once I have used the above workaround to build the capthist object, I can't seem to fit a model that is dependent on trap covariates. I'm trying to model g0 and sigma as a product of trap type (Corral, Rub, or Opportunistic) with the model structure as "model = list(g0 = ~ kcov, sigma = ~ kcov). The models appear to run fine but then when i ask for output i get the error "Error in covariates(traps(object$capthist))[, 1] : incorrect number of dimensions". I've tried several different model structure formulations and each yield the same issue.

Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Luke

messages.subject: Transect polygon design
messages.body_plain:
Hey-

I am new to SCR and secr (but not statistics or R) and I'm struggling a bit with an appropriate approach for analyzing data using fecal pellet DNA on deer and was hoping folks more familiar with SCR may be able to provide some insight.

Study Design
Deer are not territorial and typically do not congregate during the sampling period.  Winter home range size is about 186 ha.

Observers walked 200-m transects in three primary forest treatment types (6 discrete patches per treatment type) looking for fecal pellets.  Transect starting location and azimuth were selected randomly within a habitat patch and an observer walked 100 m, added 90 degrees to the azimuth and walked another 100 m.  However, if an observer happened upon a game trail, they followed the trail until they had walked a total length of 200 m or the trail forked - at which point they took the path closest to the pre-determined azimuth.  Transect routes were not recorded via GPS, but the start, mid, and endpoints as well as locations of fecal pellets were recorded.

Transects, however, were not repeated exactly.  Rather, in each of 4 occasions (spaced ~10-days apart) observers selected a new starting location and azimuth based on a random distance (1-200 m) from the habitat patch edge.  Because of this some transects intersect and others are merely clustered in close proximity to one another within the habitat patch.  The result was fairly uniform coverage (across all sampling occasions) of habitat patches.

The design, then, can be viewed as a fixed search path (i.e., protocol 1a; page 383 of Royal et al. 2014), and maybe with uniform search intensity (if viewed as a random sample of the area within the plot), but for the transects where a trail was encountered (maybe 30% of transects), they violated the assumption that the survey path is determined independent of activity centers of individuals.  Therefore, perhaps an unstructured spatial survey is a more appropriate description?

My question is how best to model these data in secr.  Right now I have it set up as a polygon search with four occasions.  However, I don't think that addresses the opportunistic searches.  I'm wondering if discretizing the polygons into smaller grid cells and then treating those cells as effective traps would address the opportunistic paths followed on some transects (similar to Bayesian methods employed by Thompson et al. 2012)?  I can also try polygons and discretized detectors and see if it matters, but my shallow knowledge of SCR makes me wonder if I'm missing something more fundamental. These data might be better modeled via Bayesian methods, but my collaborators are continuing the study and would like to use secr for subsequent analyses.

Any thoughts would be welcome.  Thanks!

Royle, J. A., R. B. handler, R. Solmann, and B. Gardner. 2014. Spatial Catpure-Recapture. Elsevier.
Thompson, C.M., J. A. Royle, and J. D. Garner. 2012. A framework for inference about carnivore density from unstructured spatial sampling of scat using detector dogs. JWM 76:863-871
